solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: One ruminating in store about caps on salad oil

indicators.note: the store wraps around the other letters, as about means surrounding

parts.note: a bin is a container for storing things

indicators.note: caps are the tops of the next two words, so their first letters are taken

explanation.surface: Someone thinking over a salad dressing while browsing in a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One ruminating' reads as a person deep in thought, but ruminants chew the cud.
explanation.definitionFit: A bison is a cud-chewing animal, and ruminating literally means chewing the cud.

clue.text: Attraction of island featuring in commercial he's broadcasting

indicators.note: featuring in says the island letter appears inside the following phrase

parts.note: an ad is a commercial advertisement
taken as written without the apostrophe
a programme being broadcast is on, or on air

explanation.surface: An islander appears in a TV advert that a man is presenting, and it proves attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcasting' looks like an anagram signal but simply gives ON, as in on air.
explanation.definitionFit: Adhesion is the force by which things stick together, a physical attraction between surfaces.

clue.text: Asian workers we separately engage?

indicators.note: the two parts of we are kept apart and take in the workers between them

parts.note: we is you and I, here the old plural you, ye, plus I
men are workers, as in management and men

explanation.surface: A question about whether we should hire workers one at a time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we' is taken as the old plural you plus I, and 'separately' means its two halves are split to take in the workers.
explanation.definitionFit: A Yemeni comes from Yemen, a country on the Arabian peninsula in Asia.

clue.text: That's Spike showing up — attention-seeker!

indicators.note: up in a down clue says the letters are read from bottom to top
showing says the letters are on display inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone pointing out Spike as he appears, calling him a show-off.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft gave the hidden run no indicator: 'showing' displays TSSP inside 'That's Spike' and 'up' turns it, as this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The whispered interjection is uttered to catch someone's notice discreetly.

clue.text: A thick-skinned generation: unfeeling, old, ignored

indicators.note: ignored says the old letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: a callous person is unfeeling and hard-hearted

explanation.surface: A complaint that a whole generation is insensitive and that the elderly are neglected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thick-skinned' looks like an insult about people but is literal: hardened skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A callus is a patch of skin grown hard and thick, so it is something the body produces as thickened tissue.

clue.text: Good glue effective, given time, for severed connection

indicators.note: effective hints at the letters being put into effect in a new arrangement

parts.note: the fodder letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: Good glue works, given time to set, to mend a broken join.
explanation.walkthrough: 'effective' is the anagram signal; T joins the letters of GOOD GLUE before they are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Signing off a computer system ends your session, cutting the link to it.

clue.text: Fowls providing eggs, see, without bits of grotty straw?

parts.words: eggs, see, without bits of grotty straw?
parts.note: take the first letters of grotty and straw out of eggs see to leave EGSEE, which is the second word of the answer jumbled, the first word being the signal for that jumbling

explanation.surface: Birds laying eggs in the wild, with no grubby straw nest to sit in.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse-style device: removing G and S from EGGS SEE leaves EGSEE, which is a wild version of the bird name in the answer, wild acting as an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Untamed migrating birds such as greylags are plural fowls of the open marsh.

clue.text: Pack and move fairly quickly, without last of paraphernalia

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the trotting word goes round the letter

parts.note: to trot is to move at a pace between a walk and a run

indicators.note: last of takes the final letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Instructions to pack up and hurry off without the last of your gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pack' looks like a verb but is the noun, and 'without' means outside, not lacking.
explanation.definitionFit: A set of fortune-telling cards is a pack, as a deck of playing cards is.

clue.text: Had tea, possibly?

parts.note: having tea could mean dining in a cafe rather than at home, and the letters of had (ate) are also tea jumbled, out of order

explanation.surface: A simple query about whether someone had their tea.
explanation.walkthrough: A second reading: ATE is 'tea' put out of order, signalled by 'possibly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a meal at a restaurant rather than home is to dine away, so tea taken in a cafe fits.

clue.text: Benedict agreed on the whole he was a strapping vegetarian!

parts.note: Benedict XVI was the Pope when this puzzle appeared

indicators.note: on the whole suggests most of the word, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: yes is the word of agreement

explanation.surface: The Pontiff agreed that, overall, here was a burly man who ate no meat.
explanation.walkthrough: The cartoon sailor got his strength from spinach, hence the joking 'vegetarian'.
explanation.definitionFit: The muscular cartoon sailor famously ate spinach to grow strong, so is jokingly called a vegetable eater.

clue.text: Charge for some substitute lager

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Asking what a pub charges for a replacement pint of lager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' looks like a price, but means care or guardianship.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in your charge is under your guardianship and instruction, a sense of being tutored.

clue.text: Admire Italian's figures

parts.note: dig is slang for like or admire
IT is the abbreviation for Italian, plus the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: Praising the shapely figures of Italian people.
explanation.definitionFit: Numerals are figures, and the ten symbols 0 to 9 are each counted on fingers.

clue.text: Utter fudge, perhaps, Chambers?

indicators.note: utter means say out loud, so the word is taken by its spoken form

parts.note: fudge is an example of a confectionery item, a sweet

explanation.surface: Accusing the Chambers dictionary of complete nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chambers' looks like the British dictionary; 'Utter fudge' looks like complete nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: A suite is a set of connected rooms, as in a hotel, so chambers fits.

clue.text: No limits to deliberate legal position

indicators.note: no limits says the outside letters of the word are removed

parts.note: to deliberate is to consider carefully

explanation.surface: There is no end to the deliberations of the law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'legal position' looks like a matter of law, but is football: not offside.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a player is in a permitted position when not offside, so legal positioning on the pitch.

clue.text: Setter's concert put off? Snap!

parts.note: the setter is I, so setter's is I'm, I am
a prom is a promenade concert

indicators.note: off suggests the letters are disturbed, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: The puzzle-maker's concert is postponed, an announcement made on a whim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snap!' looks like an exclamation of anger but is an adjective, as in a snap decision.
explanation.definitionFit: A snap judgement is made on the spur of the moment, unrehearsed and spontaneous.

clue.text: Warning, ladies — head off!

indicators.note: head off says the first letter of the word is removed

parts.note: ladies are women

explanation.surface: A warning to ladies to clear off.
explanation.definitionFit: A portent or sign of what is to come serves as a warning of the future.

clue.text: Believer and idealist after conversion, Muhammad retires

indicators.note: conversion says the letters are changed into a new order

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written
Muhammad Ali was the famous boxer

explanation.surface: An idealist converts to a faith, and a man named Muhammad withdraws.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retires' says ALI leaves the letters of IDEALIST; the rest are then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A believer in a creator God who does not intervene holds a rational faith, still a believer.

clue.text: Row bow for Goldie on outskirts of Henley — in this?

definitions.text: Row bow for Goldie on outskirts of Henley — in this?

parts.note: a din is a row, a loud noise

indicators.note: the bow is the front of the boat, so the first letter of the word
outskirts are the outer edges, so the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Wondering whether Goldie rows at the edge of the Henley regatta in a little boat.
explanation.walkthrough: Goldie is the Cambridge reserve crew; Henley is the famous rowing regatta on the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: A small rowing boat could carry someone around the edges of the regatta course.

clue.text: Join on one condition

parts.note: a means one
but introduces a condition or reservation, as in no ifs or buts

explanation.surface: Being allowed to join on a single condition.
explanation.definitionFit: To border something is to be next to it, touching or joined at an edge.

clue.text: Caffeine could be making Ada ill, OK?

indicators.note: making says these letters are being made into something new

parts.note: the fodder letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking if the coffee is making Ada unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: Caffeine is one example of the nitrogen-containing plant compounds, like nicotine and morphine.

clue.text: Goitre pangs reduced? That's an old saw!

indicators.note: reduced says the phrase is cut down to some of its letters

explanation.surface: A shrinking goitre and its aches, dismissed as a well-worn saying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'an old saw' looks like a proverb but is a surgical tool for cutting into the skull.
explanation.definitionFit: A cylindrical surgical saw formerly used to bore into bone is the instrument meant.

clue.text: Agincourt soldier's weapon?

definitions.meaning: the swaggering soldier of that name in Shakespeare's Henry V, the play about Agincourt

explanation.surface: A question about the arms carried in the medieval battle.
explanation.walkthrough: Firearms of this kind did not exist at Agincourt; the soldier is the swaggering character in Shakespeare, and 's stands for is.
explanation.definitionFit: A handgun is a weapon, and the character of that name serves in Henry V's army.

clue.text: Utterance of one in search of principle?

definitions.text: Utterance of one in search of principle?

parts.words: Utterance of one in search of principle?
parts.note: Archimedes shouted this Greek word, I have found it, on discovering his principle of displacement

explanation.surface: What a person seeking moral principles might say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'principle' looks moral but is Archimedes' principle of buoyancy, found in his bath.
explanation.definitionFit: Archimedes' cry of discovery came when he grasped the law of displacement.

clue.text: Coat worn in flagrant disregard of extremities

indicators.note: worn suggests the letters are battered into a different shape
the end letters of the word are ignored, keeping its middle

explanation.surface: A coat worn in open defiance of the rules about hands and feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disregard of extremities' trims F and T, leaving LAGRAN, which 'worn' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: An overcoat with sleeves running up to the collar, named after Lord Raglan.

clue.text: Put one's foot down for a civilian's inclusion?

parts.note: a vicar, abbreviated VIC, read upwards gives CIV, the letters at the start of civilian

explanation.surface: Taking a firm stand about letting a civilian in.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as instructions, REV (vicar) UP (turned round in a down clue) gives CIV, included in civilian.
explanation.definitionFit: To press the accelerator hard makes the engine race, so it is to put the foot down.

clue.text: His maths result's a great success

indicators.note: result is what the letters come out as when reworked, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A boy's maths results are a triumph.
explanation.definitionFit: A hugely popular record or show is a triumph, a big hit with the public.

clue.text: Cuppa with slice of madeira on the side

parts.note: a cuppa is a cup of tea

indicators.note: a slice of the word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A cup of tea with a piece of Madeira cake on the side.
explanation.walkthrough: Madeira cake is a plain British sponge served with tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A side in sport is a group of players, as in picking a side for football.

clue.text: Proof of delay when returning with 'Magic Line'

indicators.note: returning says the delay word is turned back to front

parts.note: a lag is a delay
a ley line is an alignment of ancient sites credited with mystical power

explanation.surface: Evidence of a hold-up coming back from the Magic Circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proof' looks like evidence but is a printer's trial print.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial printing of type set in long columns is a printer's proof.

clue.text: Sink or basin?

definitions.meaning: to sink low, bending or lowering oneself
a variant of stoup, a basin for holy water in a church

explanation.surface: A question about which bathroom fitting to choose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sink' looks like the basin's twin but is a verb: to lower oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: To lower oneself morally is to sink; the font for holy water is a basin.

clue.text: Perceptive story: 'Constant Promises'

parts.note: a saga is a long story
c is the symbol for the constant speed of light
IOUs are written promises to pay

explanation.surface: The title of a tale about promises that are kept.
explanation.definitionFit: A wise person shows shrewd judgement and keen discernment.
